subject: 약속은 왜 구속하는가
title: Where the force of a promise comes from
content: A promise creates an obligation out of nothing but words. Before I speak I am free to act as I please; afterwards I am bound, and my freedom has been narrowed by my own voice. Philosophers have long asked what gives such utterances their moral force, because nothing observable changes when the words are said. One familiar answer appeals to expectation. My promise leads you to rely upon me, you arrange your affairs accordingly, and breaking my word therefore damages someone who acted reasonably. This explanation captures much of what is wrong with betrayal, although it does not capture everything. A promise nobody has yet relied upon still binds, and secretly compensating you for the harm does not seem to discharge the obligation. A second answer appeals to a shared practice. Promising exists because a community maintains a convention of holding people to their word, and the value of that convention lies in making cooperation possible among those who cannot watch each other. On this view my obligation derives from participating in an institution whose benefits I accept. Although the account explains the general practice well, it explains a particular case less well, since the convention would survive my single defection. A third answer locates the force in what I did to myself. By promising I invited you to trust me, and having issued that invitation I cannot withdraw it without treating you as someone whose reliance does not matter. The wrong is not the damage but the contempt. What all three accounts share is a refusal to treat a promise as a mere prediction about future behaviour. A prediction that proves false was simply mistaken; a promise that proves false was violated, and the difference between those two verdicts is the whole moral content of the practice. Any adequate philosophy of obligation must explain why words alone can produce a genuine constraint upon action.

subject: 비밀을 지킬 의무
title: When you may not tell what you know
content: Somebody tells you something and asks you to keep it. From that moment you hold knowledge you may not use freely, and the moral constraint operates even where disclosure would harm nobody. Understanding why requires asking what a confidence actually is, since the obligation cannot rest on consequences alone. One account grounds the duty in the promise that usually accompanies the telling. Yet secrets bind even when no promise was uttered, because the circumstances of the telling carried an implicit assurance. A doctor, a friend, or a lawyer receives information under conditions everyone understands, therefore the obligation arises from the relationship rather than from any explicit words. A deeper account attends to what the discloser gave up. Information about oneself is among the few things a person genuinely controls, and telling somebody surrenders that control on the understanding that it will be exercised as if it had never left. Betraying a confidence is therefore not merely unhelpful; it takes something back from a person who handed it over in trust. The value at stake is closer to autonomy than to comfort. The limits of the duty follow from the same reasoning. Where keeping a secret would permit serious harm to a third party, the obligation weakens, since the discloser cannot use another person's trust to purchase protection for wrongdoing. Professional codes reflect this judgment, although they draw the boundary at different places, and the disagreement is a genuine moral disagreement rather than a technical one. What makes such cases difficult is that both considerations are real. Breaking a confidence damages an institution that many people depend upon, and keeping one may leave somebody exposed. Neither side can be dismissed as sentimentality, therefore the right response is to weigh them openly rather than to pretend that one obviously dominates. Confidentiality is a genuine value with genuine limits, and both halves of that truth deserve attention.

subject: 용서는 무엇을 지우는가
title: What forgiveness actually cancels
content: Forgiveness is praised almost everywhere, and yet its moral structure is puzzling. If a wrong was genuinely committed, forgiving cannot make it undone, and pretending otherwise would be a falsehood rather than a virtue. So what exactly does the forgiver give up, and why should giving it up be admirable? One answer says that forgiveness releases a debt. On this reading the wrongdoer owes something, and the injured party may cancel the claim just as a creditor may cancel a loan. The analogy explains why only the person wronged can forgive, since nobody may discharge a debt owed to somebody else. It explains rather less about wrongs that cannot be repaid, where the language of debt strains badly. A better account concerns the attitude rather than any claim. To forgive is to give up resentment toward the wrongdoer while continuing to hold that the act was wrong. This is why forgiveness differs from excusing and from forgetting. Excusing denies that a genuine wrong occurred; forgetting removes the knowledge; forgiveness keeps the moral judgment intact and changes only the stance toward the person. Understood this way, the value of forgiveness becomes clearer. Resentment holds the injured party fast to the worst hour of their life, and releasing it restores something that the original wrong had taken. Therefore forgiveness serves the forgiver as much as the forgiven, although describing it purely as self interest would miss the moral relation involved. Two cautions follow. Forgiveness offered too quickly can signal that the wrong mattered little, which insults the truth about what happened. And nobody may be obliged to forgive, since demanding it from a victim adds a further burden to whatever they already carry. What can be said is that forgiveness, when it comes freely and with the judgment intact, is among the more difficult things a person may achieve.

subject: 신뢰를 저버린다는 것
title: Why breaking trust is a distinct wrong
content: Being let down by somebody who never promised anything is disappointing. Being let down by somebody who was trusted is different in kind, and the moral difference deserves examination, because it explains why betrayal wounds in a way that mere failure does not. Trust involves accepting vulnerability. When I trust you, I place something within your power and stop guarding it, therefore I have made myself worse off in the event that you fail me. That deliberate lowering of defences is the whole point, since a relation in which each party watched the other continually would not be trust at all. It would be surveillance with better manners. What follows is that the truster has done something, not merely predicted something. To trust is to hold an expectation about your conduct and also to signal that I regard you as the kind of person who answers such expectations. Consequently a betrayal denies both. It disappoints the expectation, and it rejects the standing I offered, which is why the injured party frequently reports feeling foolish as well as harmed. Justice between individuals depends heavily upon this practice. Contracts and laws cover only a fraction of what people rely upon, and the remainder rests on the willingness to be exposed without a remedy. A society where that willingness collapses must substitute enforcement everywhere, which is expensive, slow, and never complete. Therefore breaking trust damages more than one relationship. Rebuilding it is correspondingly difficult. An apology addresses the act, yet what was broken is a belief about the person, and beliefs of that kind are revised slowly and through evidence rather than through words. The wrongdoer cannot simply restore what existed before, because the truster now knows something they did not know, and no argument can return them to their earlier ignorance.

subject: 충성과 도덕의 충돌
title: When loyalty asks for something wrong
content: Loyalty is counted a virtue in nearly every tradition, and yet it regularly collides with other moral demands. Somebody may be loyal to a friend, a family, a firm, or a country, and each of these attachments can require conduct that impartial justice would forbid. Understanding the collision requires seeing what loyalty is actually good for. Its value lies in constancy under pressure. A person who abandons an attachment whenever a better option appears has attachments in name only, and the goods that require time — friendship, institutions, long collaboration — depend upon people who stay. Therefore loyalty is not merely a sentiment; it is the disposition that makes certain valuable relations possible at all. The difficulty is that the same disposition resists moral revision. If loyalty means standing by somebody regardless of what they do, it becomes a licence for anything, and appeals to it have excused a great deal of serious wrongdoing. Whistleblowers are frequently condemned as disloyal by people who do not dispute the truth of what they revealed, which shows how readily the virtue is used to suppress it. A defensible account sets loyalty inside limits rather than above them. What the virtue requires is that I give the person or institution more attention, more patience, and more benefit of the doubt than a stranger would receive. What it does not require is that I help them do wrong or conceal what they did. Read this way, exposing a corrupt employer is not disloyalty but a demanding form of it. Where the two genuinely conflict, the moral argument favours the wider claim. My attachments are mine and matter enormously, yet a third party harmed by my loyalty never agreed to bear that cost, and no account of justice can ask them to.

subject: 처벌은 무엇을 위한 것인가
title: What punishment is supposed to accomplish
content: Punishment deliberately imposes suffering upon somebody, which is exactly what morality ordinarily forbids. Any justification must therefore explain what makes this particular infliction permissible, and the competing answers pull in different directions. One tradition looks backward. The wrongdoer deserves to suffer because of what they did, and the punishment restores a moral balance that the offence disturbed. This view captures a strong intuition, since most people believe that a serious wrong should not simply pass. Yet it is hard to say what the balance consists of, or why adding a second harm should repair the first. A second tradition looks forward. Punishment is justified by its effects: it deters others, restrains the dangerous, and may reform the offender. This account has the advantage of asking for evidence rather than for metaphysics. It has a notorious difficulty as well, because if only effects matter, then punishing somebody known to be innocent would be permissible whenever it deterred effectively, and that conclusion should be rejected outright. Most defensible positions combine the two. Desert sets the limit while consequences supply the purpose, so nobody may be punished who does not deserve it, and among permissible punishments we choose those that actually help. This arrangement respects the moral standing of the offender while keeping the practice answerable to results. What the argument makes plain is how much current practice depends upon unexamined assumptions. Sentences frequently exceed what deterrence requires and what reform can use, and the excess is justified by appeals to desert that nobody can measure. Where a practice imposes deliberate suffering, the burden of justification should be heavy, and any element that serves neither desert nor any demonstrated effect deserves the plainest possible name: it is harm without a reason.

subject: 사면의 논리
title: The strange power to set a penalty aside
content: Almost every legal order reserves a power to cancel a punishment that was lawfully imposed. This seems paradoxical, since if the verdict was correct then setting it aside defeats justice, and if it was incorrect then the remedy should be appeal rather than mercy. Examining the paradox reveals something about the limits of rules. One justification treats the power as a correction. Rules are general, cases are particular, and occasionally a correct application produces an outcome that everybody recognises as monstrous. No system of rules can anticipate every situation, therefore a residual authority to depart from the result serves the purposes that the rules themselves were meant to advance. On this reading mercy is not opposed to justice but completes it. A second justification concerns change over time. A punishment fixed years ago may have been proportionate then and appear excessive now, because moral views shift and the offender may have become a different person. Releasing them acknowledges that the judgment attached to a moment rather than to eternity. Although this reasoning is sound, it invites the objection that the same argument would license constant revision. The serious danger lies in who exercises the power. Historically it has belonged to rulers, and rulers have used it to reward allies, to buy loyalty, and to shield associates from consequences that ordinary people bear. Where that happens, the exception corrodes the very principle it was supposed to serve, since it demonstrates that the law binds only those without access. Therefore the moral case for such a power depends almost entirely on constraints around it. Reasons stated publicly, decisions reviewable by others, and criteria applied consistently transform an arbitrary favour into a defensible institution. Without those constraints the power is not mercy at all but privilege wearing its clothes.

subject: 무지의 책임
title: When not knowing is no defence
content: People frequently excuse themselves by saying they did not know. Sometimes the excuse is entirely proper, since nobody can be blamed for failing to act on information that was genuinely unavailable. Yet in many cases ignorance itself is the thing we blame, and understanding the difference is a central problem in moral philosophy. The key question is whether the person could reasonably have known. A driver who did not notice a warning light is not excused if checking was part of the job, and an employer who never asked where their materials came from cannot claim innocence about conditions they preferred not to discover. In such cases the failure occurred earlier, at the moment when a reasonable person would have inquired. Therefore the blame attaches to the inquiry rather than to the act. This explains a phenomenon that is otherwise puzzling. People often arrange not to know things, avoiding the question whose answer would create an obligation, and such deliberate avoidance is worse rather than better than knowing. Somebody who investigates and then acts wrongly at least confronted the truth; somebody who declined to look has used ignorance as an instrument. The moral verdict should track that difference. Setting the standard is genuinely difficult. Requiring everyone to know everything would be impossible, and blame would become universal and therefore meaningless. A workable principle asks what inquiry the situation demanded, weighing the seriousness of the possible harm against the cost of finding out. Where the stakes are high and the inquiry is cheap, not knowing is a failure. What follows in practice is a duty that receives too little attention. Alongside the familiar obligations to avoid harm and keep promises sits a quieter one to inform oneself, and a great deal of ordinary wrongdoing consists in nothing more than never having asked.

subject: 의지박약의 문제
title: Acting against your own better judgment
content: People regularly do what they believe they should not do. They judge that one course is better, they are not compelled, and they choose the other anyway. Philosophers have found this ordinary experience remarkably hard to explain, because it seems to require that somebody knowingly choose the worse option, and that looks close to impossible. One ancient response denies the phenomenon. If a person genuinely knew that an action was worse, they would not perform it, therefore whenever they act badly their knowledge must have failed at the moment of choice. On this view moral failure is always a failure of understanding. The account is elegant, although it collides with the plain experience of doing something while fully aware of its foolishness. A second response distinguishes types of judgment. I may hold a general belief that late nights damage my work while the immediate attraction organises my attention so completely that the general belief plays no part. The knowledge is present but inert, therefore the choice is not made against an operative judgment at all. This explanation preserves both the truth of the belief and the reality of the failure. A third response focuses on time. Value that arrives sooner looms larger than value arriving later, so a person may prefer the greater good when both are distant and reverse that preference as the smaller one approaches. Nothing irrational occurs at any single moment; the inconsistency appears only across the sequence. What follows for practice is more useful than the theoretical dispute. If weakness of will arises from attention and timing rather than from ignorance, then arguing with oneself at the moment of temptation is the least effective remedy. Arranging matters in advance works better, since the choice made calmly binds the person who will not be calm.

subject: 아직 태어나지 않은 사람들
title: Owing something to people who do not yet exist
content: Decisions taken now will determine the conditions under which future generations live. Whether we owe them anything is a genuine philosophical question, since the beneficiaries of our restraint do not yet exist and cannot claim, complain, or consent. Several familiar moral concepts fit such cases badly. Rights ordinarily belong to somebody in particular, and no particular person can be identified among those who will exist a century hence. Worse, the identity of future people depends upon what we do, because different policies produce different populations. Therefore we cannot say that a specific future person will be harmed by our choices, since under a different policy that person would never have been born at all. This puzzle has troubled every attempt to state the obligation precisely. Yet the conclusion that we owe nothing should be rejected. It implies that leaving a poisoned world would wrong nobody, provided the inhabitants owe their existence to the same decisions, and almost nobody accepts that result. The obvious wrongness of such conduct is better evidence than any argument that denies it. One promising reformulation shifts from persons to conditions. We may owe it to the future that whoever exists then should find a world in which a decent life remains available, without needing to name who they are. This treats the obligation as attaching to the state of the world rather than to any claimant, which sidesteps the identity problem entirely. What the argument establishes is that our moral vocabulary was built for contemporaries and strains when extended across generations. That strain is a reason to develop the vocabulary rather than to abandon the obligation, because the practical question will not wait. Choices about climate, resources, and knowledge are being made now, and their effects will outlast every person capable of debating them.

subject: 유언은 왜 존중되는가
title: Honouring the wishes of the dead
content: We treat the instructions of the dead as binding to a remarkable degree. Property is distributed according to documents written by people who no longer exist, and courts enforce those directions against the living. Since the dead cannot be benefited or harmed in any obvious way, the practice invites a genuine philosophical question. One justification looks to the living. Knowing that my wishes will be honoured after my death lets me plan a life that extends beyond it, and such projects — endowing a school, providing for a child, completing a body of work — are among the things that make a life feel whole. Therefore the practice serves people while they are alive, and the enforcement afterwards is what makes the earlier assurance credible. A second justification appeals to the moral standing of the person who wrote. What somebody owned was theirs, and the freedom to determine its fate is part of what owning meant. On this reading disregarding a will would be a kind of retrospective confiscation, taking from the person the very control that property was supposed to supply. The considerations on the other side are also strong. The dead cannot revise their instructions in light of changed circumstances, so a document written decades ago may direct resources toward purposes now useless or offensive. Every legal system therefore limits the power, refusing to enforce conditions that are cruel, impossible, or contrary to justice, and most restrict how far into the future control may reach. What emerges is a practice justified by its effect on the living rather than by any duty owed to the deceased. That conclusion has a practical consequence. Where honouring a will would seriously harm those who remain, the moral case for enforcement weakens, because the value being protected was never really the wish itself.

subject: 동의가 하는 일
title: How agreement changes what is permitted
content: Consent performs a remarkable moral transformation. An act that would be a serious wrong becomes permissible because somebody agreed to it, and nothing else about the act need change. Surgery, contact sports, and lending money all depend upon this power, therefore understanding its conditions matters a great deal. The transformation works because certain moral protections belong to the person protected. My claim against being touched is mine to waive, so waiving it removes the wrong rather than outweighing it. This explains why consent operates differently from justification: a justified act was still an interference that required defending, whereas a consented act involved no interference at all. Yet the power has conditions, and most disputes concern them rather than the principle. Agreement given without relevant information does not transfer the moral protection, since the person waived a claim they did not understand. Agreement given under threat is not agreement, because the alternative was arranged by the very party seeking it. And agreement given by somebody unable to weigh the matter cannot carry the moral weight, which is why capacity questions are so difficult in medicine. A further limit concerns what may be waived at all. Most traditions hold that certain protections cannot be surrendered even willingly, and the argument for that position appeals to values beyond individual choice. Whether such limits are justified remains genuinely contested, since they override a person's own judgment about their own life. What the whole structure reveals is that consent is not a formality but the moral hinge of an enormous range of ordinary conduct. Treating it as a signature obtained rather than an understanding reached empties it of the very thing that gave it force, and a great deal of institutional practice makes exactly that mistake.

subject: 필요와 권리의 구분
title: Between what somebody needs and what they may claim
content: That a person needs something and that they have a right to it are different claims, and confusing them causes considerable trouble in moral argument. A need describes a condition of the person: without this, they suffer, fail, or die. A right describes a relation between people: somebody is required to supply it, and failing to do so is a wrong rather than a misfortune. The distinction matters because rights carry addresses. If I have a right to medical care, then somebody in particular must provide it, and identifying who bears that duty is part of stating the claim. Needs carry no such address on their own, therefore moving from need to right requires an argument about who should bear the cost and why. Skipping that argument produces claims that sound urgent while telling nobody what to do. Yet the distinction should not be used to dismiss needs. A serious unmet need is a moral fact, and the absence of an identified duty-bearer is a defect in our institutions rather than a reason for indifference. Where a need is grave, widely shared, and could be met at reasonable cost, that combination is itself the beginning of an argument for creating the corresponding obligation. Justice frequently consists in constructing such arrangements where none existed. Two errors follow from collapsing the two ideas. Treating every need as an existing right invites cynicism when the right proves unenforceable, and treating rights as nothing more than urgent needs deprives them of the force that makes them useful. Rights work precisely because they resist the ordinary weighing of interests, and that resistance is purchased by their being definite. What careful moral argument requires, then, is patience about the middle step. From the truth that somebody needs something, the question is what follows, and answering it honestly is more useful than asserting the conclusion loudly.

subject: 원조의 의무는 어디까지인가
title: How much a stranger's suffering can demand
content: If somebody drowning could be saved at trivial cost, almost everybody agrees that failing to help is seriously wrong. A well known moral argument extends that judgment: distance makes no difference to the value of a life, therefore preventable suffering far away generates the same obligation, and most of us are failing continuously. The argument is uncomfortable precisely because each step looks correct. Distance genuinely seems morally irrelevant, and the claim that we should prevent great harm at small cost is difficult to reject. Yet the conclusion appears to demand almost unlimited sacrifice, since further suffering always remains, and a moral theory requiring everything from everybody is regarded by many as evidence against itself. Several responses have been offered. One denies that the cases are alike, pointing out that the drowning child presents a clear act with a certain result, whereas distant aid passes through institutions whose effects are uncertain. This is a genuine consideration although it argues for choosing carefully rather than for doing nothing. A second response appeals to the difference between what is required and what is admirable, holding that great sacrifice is praiseworthy without being obligatory. That distinction has real moral weight, yet it is suspiciously convenient for those who invoke it. A third response emphasises collective arrangements. If the problem is of a scale that no individual can address, the primary obligation may be to support institutions that can, rather than to give until nothing remains. This shifts the demand from personal sacrifice to political action without denying the underlying claim. What survives every response is the core judgment. Suffering that could be prevented at moderate cost presents a genuine moral demand, and the debate concerns how much and through what means, not whether anything is owed at all.

subject: 난민에 대한 의무
title: What we owe to those who had to leave
content: Somebody who flees persecution arrives at a border and asks to be admitted. The question of what is owed to them has generated a large moral literature, because it sits at the intersection of two claims that both seem valid. A political community appears entitled to decide who joins it, and a person in serious danger appears entitled to protection. One position begins from the danger. If somebody faces persecution, and admitting them would prevent it at moderate cost, then refusing is not merely ungenerous but a serious wrong. On this reading the obligation resembles the duty to rescue, and the fact that the person arrived at a particular border is morally accidental. Their need, rather than any relationship, generates the claim. A second position begins from the community. Members share institutions, obligations, and a common life, and deciding together who else may join is part of governing themselves. Removing that decision would take something genuinely valuable from people who did nothing wrong. Although this argument has force, its force diminishes sharply as the stakes on the other side rise, since no account of self government explains a right to exclude somebody who will otherwise die. Most careful positions therefore combine the claims asymmetrically. A community retains wide discretion over ordinary immigration and very little over those fleeing serious harm, because the moral weight of the two cases differs enormously. The difficult questions concern the middle: what counts as serious enough, and how a burden falling unevenly upon nearby countries should be shared. What the argument makes clear is that the obligation cannot be discharged by declaring a general willingness. Justice here is measured in places actually offered, and a state whose stated principles exceed its practice has answered the moral question in deeds rather than in words.

subject: 표현의 자유와 해악
title: Where speech stops being merely speech
content: Freedom of expression is defended by arguments of unusual strength. Suppressing an opinion assumes we already know it to be false, silencing dissent deprives the majority of the chance to test its own beliefs, and any authority empowered to decide what may be said will eventually protect itself. These considerations explain why the value is treated as close to fundamental. Yet no defender has ever held that speech is entirely without limits. Fraud, incitement, and threats are speech, and prohibiting them provokes no serious moral objection, therefore the real argument concerns where the boundary falls rather than whether one exists. The standard proposal locates it at harm, permitting restriction only where expression causes injury rather than mere offence. That formulation does considerable work while leaving the hardest cases open. Offence and harm are not always separable, since sustained contempt directed at a group can damage the standing of its members in ways that resemble injury more than discomfort. Defenders of a narrow boundary reply that expanding the category invites exactly the authority the original argument warned against, because whoever decides which speech wounds will decide in their own interest. Both concerns are genuine, and no formula dissolves the tension. What the debate frequently overlooks is that the strongest arguments for the freedom are arguments about truth and about power rather than about self expression. They protect the dissenter, the researcher, and the critic, and they apply with far less force to speech that contributes nothing to any inquiry. Recognising this narrows the dispute usefully. The moral question is not whether people may say whatever they like, but which protections a society must maintain so that its beliefs remain open to correction, and that question has a more definite answer than the broader one.

subject: 사생활은 왜 가치 있는가
title: What is lost when nothing is private
content: Privacy is frequently defended on the ground that people have something to hide, which concedes far too much. A stronger moral argument holds that privacy protects goods available to somebody with nothing whatever to conceal, and identifying those goods explains why the value survives even where wrongdoing is absent. The first good concerns relationships. What distinguishes a friend from an acquaintance is partly what they know, therefore a person who is equally transparent to everybody has lost the ability to make anyone close. Intimacy is constituted by selective disclosure, so removing the selection removes the intimacy. This alone establishes that privacy is not merely a shield against embarrassment. The second good concerns development. Working out what one believes requires trying positions that may prove foolish, and doing that under observation is far harder, because every provisional thought becomes a record. A person permanently watched tends toward whatever is already approved, which is a genuine loss both to them and to the wider search for truth. The third good concerns power. Information about somebody is an instrument for influencing them, and the party holding it gains an advantage they need never exercise openly. Even where nobody acts on what they know, the awareness of being known alters behaviour, and that alteration has not been consented to. Justice between unequal parties depends heavily upon limiting such asymmetries. What these arguments share is that they do not depend on secrecy about misconduct. A person with an entirely blameless life still needs to choose who knows what, still needs unobserved room to think, and still has reason to object when institutions accumulate detail about them. Framing privacy as the interest of wrongdoers concedes the moral high ground at the outset and misdescribes what is actually at stake.

subject: 익명성의 도덕
title: Speaking without attaching your name
content: Anonymity permits somebody to act or speak without being identified, and moral judgments about it swing sharply depending on the example chosen. The anonymous whistleblower and the anonymous abuser both rely on the same condition, therefore any adequate account must explain what makes the practice valuable in one case and corrosive in the other. The value is clearest where speech carries risk. A person reporting corruption, describing persecution, or dissenting under an authority that punishes dissent can act only if identification is prevented. In such cases anonymity protects the flow of truth against those with power to suppress it, and a society that eliminated it would silence exactly the testimony it most needs. Voting by secret ballot rests on the same reasoning. The corrosion is equally clear. Identification is what ordinarily attaches consequences to conduct, so removing it removes a substantial part of what restrains people, and behaviour that nobody would defend in their own name becomes cheap. Moreover the audience loses information, since knowing who speaks helps in judging what they say, and an anonymous claim cannot be weighed against the speaker's interests or expertise. What distinguishes the good case from the bad is the direction of the power involved. Anonymity used by somebody vulnerable against somebody stronger protects them from retaliation. Anonymity used by somebody against a weaker party simply removes accountability that would otherwise exist. Therefore the same condition serves justice in one configuration and defeats it in the other. This suggests that blanket positions are mistaken. A rule requiring universal identification would harm those with most to fear, and a rule guaranteeing universal concealment would shield those with least excuse. Defensible arrangements attend to who is protected from whom, which is a moral question rather than a technical one.

subject: 예술의 도덕적 평가
title: Judging a work by what it recommends
content: Whether moral criticism of art is legitimate has divided philosophers for a long time. One position holds that artistic value and moral value are entirely separate, so a work may be repellent in its attitudes and superb as art, and confusing the two commits a category error. The opposing position holds that a work which invites us to endorse something vicious has failed at something internal to art itself. The separatist argument has real strength. Art frequently explores what its maker does not endorse, and demanding moral approval from every work would eliminate most serious literature, which examines cruelty precisely by presenting it. Judging works by whether their characters behave well is plainly a mistake, and the history of censorship offers ample warning about where such judgments lead. Yet the opposing case is not so easily dismissed. A work does more than depict; it arranges attention, invites sympathy, and asks the audience to feel that certain things are fitting. Where the invitation is to enjoy the humiliation of a group, the audience must either refuse the invitation or accept it, and refusing means the work has failed to do what it attempted. On this reading the moral defect produces an artistic one, since the response the work sought is unavailable to anyone who sees clearly. A moderate conclusion follows. Depicting a wrong is not endorsing it, and the distinction between representing and recommending carries most of the weight. Where a work genuinely recommends something vicious, the criticism is legitimate and concerns the work rather than its subject. Where it merely represents, the moral objection is misplaced. Making that distinction requires reading carefully rather than counting offences, which is precisely why moral criticism of art is difficult and why it is so frequently done badly.

subject: 취향에 옳고 그름이 있는가
title: Whether judgments of taste can be mistaken
content: When somebody says a work is beautiful, they seem to be doing more than reporting a preference. Preferences invite no argument, and yet disagreements about value in art are pursued with considerable energy, as though there were something to be right about. This tension has occupied philosophers for centuries. One position treats such judgments as purely subjective. Beauty describes a response in the observer rather than a property of the object, therefore two people who respond differently are both correct, and the appearance of disagreement is an illusion produced by the grammar of our sentences. The account is simple and explains why argument so rarely settles anything. It explains rather poorly why we bother arguing at all, or why the judgments of trained critics carry weight. A second position holds that some responses are better informed than others. Somebody who knows a tradition hears relations that a newcomer misses, and their judgment reflects more of what is actually present in the work. On this reading taste is not a matter of truth in the way that measurement is, and yet it admits of better and worse, because a response can be based on more or less of the object. A third consideration concerns what the judgment claims. Saying a work is beautiful appears to invite agreement rather than merely to announce a fact about oneself, which is why the judgment feels answerable to reasons. We support it by pointing at features, and pointing succeeds when the other person comes to see what we saw. What emerges is a middle position with practical value. There may be no fact settling every dispute, and yet a judgment can be uninformed, careless, or blind to what is there. Treating taste as beyond criticism removes the possibility of learning to perceive better, which is the whole point of attending to art seriously.

subject: 자연의 가치
title: Whether the wild matters apart from us
content: Arguments for protecting wild places usually appeal to human benefit. Wild systems supply clean air, medicines, and recreation, and losing them would cost us dearly. Such reasoning is effective and largely true, yet many people hold a further conviction that it fails to capture: that the loss would be regrettable even if no person were affected. Whether that conviction can be defended is a genuine philosophical question. The instrumental argument has an uncomfortable implication. If value depends entirely upon usefulness, then a wild system that served no purpose would have no claim upon us, and replacing it with something more useful would be an improvement rather than a loss. Most defenders of the wild reject that conclusion, therefore they are committed to some value that does not pass through human interests. One way of defending the further claim points to the experience of the person judging. Somebody who has attended closely to a wild place reports discovering value rather than assigning it, and although this does not prove the value is independent, dismissing such testimony requires an argument of its own. A second way notes that we make similar judgments elsewhere. We think it would be wrong to destroy a great work even if nobody would ever see it again, which suggests our moral thinking already accommodates value that nobody consumes. The practical stakes are real. An argument resting purely on usefulness will lose whenever a more profitable use appears, and conservation defended on those terms is permanently vulnerable. Recognising a value that does not depend upon our purposes changes what the argument is about, and while such a position is harder to establish, it may be the only one that actually protects what its defenders care about.

subject: 고통은 왜 나쁜가
title: What makes suffering count against something
content: Almost every moral theory treats suffering as a reason against whatever produces it. This near universal agreement conceals a genuine difficulty, since theories disagree sharply about why suffering matters, and the disagreement affects which conclusions follow. One view holds that suffering is bad in itself, requiring no further explanation. Its badness is as basic as anything in ethics, and asking what makes it bad misunderstands where explanation ends. This position has obvious appeal, because the badness does seem evident to anyone who has experienced it. Yet if suffering were simply bad wherever it occurred, then whose suffering it is would carry no weight, and that implication troubles many. A second view ties the badness to the person. What is bad is not suffering as such but somebody suffering, since it is their life that goes worse and their projects that are interrupted. On this reading moral concern attaches to persons rather than to states, which explains why we think it matters how burdens are distributed and not merely how much total suffering exists. A third view attends to what suffering does. Pain occupies attention, forecloses options, and makes other goods unavailable, therefore its badness is partly a matter of what it prevents. This account fits the observation that suffering somebody has chosen for a purpose is experienced quite differently from suffering imposed upon them. The practical differences are considerable. If only the quantity matters, then reducing the total is the whole task and distribution is irrelevant. If persons matter, then relieving concentrated suffering may take priority over relieving a larger amount spread thinly. Most people's judgments follow the second pattern, which suggests that our moral thinking about suffering is already about lives rather than about a quantity of experience.

subject: 행복과 좋은 삶
title: Whether feeling well means living well
content: It is tempting to identify a good life with a life that feels good. On such a view the moral and practical question is simply how to arrange matters so that pleasant experience predominates, and everything else is instrumental. The view is clear, measurable, and almost certainly incomplete. A well known thought experiment brings out the difficulty. Suppose a machine could supply any experience you wished, indistinguishable from reality, for as long as you lived. Most people report that they would decline, and their reason is instructive: they want to do things rather than merely to have the experience of doing them, and they want their beliefs about their own lives to be true. If experience were all that mattered, refusing would make no sense. What this suggests is that the value of a life includes its relation to the world. Achievement matters partly because something was actually achieved, friendship matters partly because somebody actually cares, and knowledge matters partly because the beliefs are true. Therefore two lives feeling identical from inside may differ in value, which no purely experiential account can allow. A second consideration concerns what the good feeling is about. Contentment resting on a false picture of oneself seems less valuable than the same contentment resting on an accurate one, and satisfaction taken in something worthless seems less valuable than satisfaction taken in something worth caring about. The object of the feeling enters the assessment. None of this shows that feeling well is unimportant. A life of achievement and truth accompanied by constant misery is not obviously going well either, and any plausible account must include how a life is experienced from within. What the arguments establish is that experience is one ingredient rather than the whole measure, and treating it as the whole leaves out most of what people actually want.

subject: 운이 도덕에 미치는 영향
title: How much of a moral verdict is luck
content: Two drivers behave identically, and one of them strikes a child who happened to step into the road. We blame that driver far more severely, sentence them differently, and they blame themselves in a way the other never will. Yet neither did anything the other did not do, which exposes a deep tension in moral thinking. The tension arises because we hold two convictions that conflict. The first says that people are responsible only for what lies within their control, since blaming somebody for what they could not affect is unjust. The second says that outcomes matter, and our actual practices of blame, punishment, and self reproach track results rather than intentions alone. Both convictions are firmly held, therefore something must give. One response defends the practice. What a person does includes what they bring about, and treating action as merely a matter of intention shrinks agency until nothing is left but inner states. On this reading the driver who caused a death did something worse, and their heavier self reproach is appropriate rather than confused. Another response defends the principle and condemns the practice. Our responses to outcomes are a psychological fact about us rather than a moral truth, so the harsher judgment reflects how vividly the harm presents itself rather than any genuine difference in what was done. Both responses face difficulties. The problem extends further than accidents, since the character somebody has, the situations they encounter, and the options available to them are all substantially matters of luck. If we subtract everything unchosen, very little remains to praise or blame. What the argument leaves is a warning rather than a solution. Moral verdicts rest on foundations less solid than they appear, and recognising this is a reason for humility in judging others rather than for abandoning judgment.
